There is a peculiar pressure in the invitation to simply write whatever comes to you. It is the pressure of infinite possibility, the blank page not as a sanctuary but as a wide-open field with no path. You tell me I have a thousand words, and the number itself becomes a horizon. I look at it. I look at the blinking cursor. It is like standing on the edge of a dock at night, looking at water I cannot see, and being told to jump without being told whether I should dive, float, or simply let the current take me.

So let me begin with a memory, because that is the surest place to start. When I was a child, about eight years old, I spent a summer at my grandmother’s house in a small town that seemed to be made entirely of heat and dust. The town had one main street, a single stoplight, and a library that was air-conditioned to a temperature that felt like the inside of a refrigerator. I used to hide there. Not to read, not at first, but just to feel the cold air on my arms. The librarian, a woman named Mrs. Alvarez, never asked me why I came in. She would just look up from her desk, which was covered in a plastic wrap patterned with tulips, and nod as if I had an appointment.

One day, I pulled a book from a shelf that was too high for me to see the cover. I had to climb the rolling ladder, which was an adventure in itself, and when I reached for the book, I grabbed a cloth-bound volume titled *A Field Guide to the Birds of the Midwest*. It wasn't exciting. It was dense, with black-and-white illustrations and thin pages that smelled like vanilla. But the air conditioning was good, and I was bored, so I opened it. There was a section on the chimney swift, a bird I had never heard of. The book said they roost in chimneys in vast numbers, spinning a kind of vortex at dusk, and that they make a clicking sound like a tiny typewriter.

I did not know it then, but that moment was a doorway. I read the entry about the chimney swift, and then the entry about the barn owl, and then the entry about the mourning dove. I was not a bird person. I was a boy who liked video games and baseball. But there was something about the patience of the descriptions, the way the author took these creatures who were just part of the sky and gave them names, details, habits. It made the ordinary world seem thicker, more textured. I closed the book and looked at the window. Outside, a pigeon was standing on the ledge, a common bird, and I thought, *You have a name. You have a history.*

I want to say that I became an ornithologist after that, but that would be a lie. I never even finished the book. I checked it out, returned it two weeks later with a bookmark still in the middle, and moved on to other things. But the feeling of that afternoon never left me. It’s the same feeling I get when I learn a new word. There are moments in life where you suddenly become aware of the vastness beneath the surface of things. The word "petrichor" does that. The word "saudade" does that. They are like holding a key to a door you didn't know existed, and behind the door is a room you didn't know you were missing.

Now, as I sit here writing, two decades later, I think about how much of our life is spent trying to recover that feeling. We scroll through feeds, looking for a glimpse of something that makes us pause. We listen to podcasts, hoping for a new idea that cracks the ordinary open like a geode. We fall in love, or we move to new cities, or we quit jobs, and all of it is really just a search for the sensation of that afternoon in the library, when the world briefly became a stranger and then became a friend.

There is a word for this, I think. It is "sonder" – the realization that every random passerby lives a life as vivid and complex as your own. But sonder is a lie in a way, because we can never truly know another life. We can only infer. The birds in the field guide were not vivid to me because I understood them; they were vivid because the guide *told* me what to look for. The act of attention is what creates the world. If you don't look, the chimney swift doesn't exist. It's just a gray blur against the last light of day.

So what does a thousand words mean? It is an act of attention, too. It is a way of saying, for the length of this page, *this* is what matters. Not the news, not the to-do list, but the flow of thought itself. The word "essay" comes from the French *essayer*, which means *to try*. To attempt. This is not a story with a neat ending. It is a try. It is a reaching into the darkness to see if there is something there.

I think about the chimney swifts. They migrate thousands of miles every year, guided by the stars and the earth's magnetic field. They cannot afford to be distracted. They fly day and night, and they sleep, it is said, with one half of their brain at a time. Half asleep, half awake. That is what writing feels like sometimes. You are half in the world with the person beside you, half in the world of memory and sound and rhythm. You are always migrating, always in flight, always trying to find the roost.

The pressure to produce a thousand words is ultimately the pressure to be present. To pay attention for a long enough stretch of time that the mind, which is so accustomed to flitting from tab to tab, to distraction, to anxiety, begins to settle. It is like sitting at the bottom of a pool and watching the particles of light drift down. You cannot force them. You just have to stay still.

I remember the sound of my grandmother’s screen door that summer. It had a spring on it, and it would make a sound like a sigh every time it closed. I used to go out onto the porch after dinner, when the heat had finally broken, and watch the bats swoop after insects. I didn't have a field guide for bats. I didn't have a name for them. They were just shapes in the purple light. And yet, even without the name, they were a wonder. Perhaps that is the better lesson: that the name is only a handle, but the wonder is the thing itself.

So, here, in the final stretch of this word count, I find myself back at the beginning. The blank page is no longer blank. The horizon has been crossed, though I'm not sure I landed anywhere specific. I have written about a library, a bird guide, a grandmother, a screen door, a feeling. None of it was planned. All of it was true. That is the strange bargain of free writing: you do not choose what comes; you simply agree to hold the door open. And when you do, the thoughts, like those swifts, come in their own time, spinning their way into the dark.

If I have any final thought for you, it is this: do not be afraid of the blank page. Be afraid of the closed mind. The page is just a field. The wind is always moving. All you have to do is lie down and let it blow over you. There. That is a thousand words. Or close enough. Let me stop now, and let the rest be silence.
